title: Association, Aggregation, and Composition
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of association, aggregation, and composition and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—object relationships—in a small, readable example.
Predict the example result and check it against the stated output or a boundary-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study association, aggregation, and composition with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you choose between inheritance, interfaces, and composition based on the relationship being modeled. In this lesson, focus on object relationships and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A class defines state and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation protects invariants by keeping mutable state private and validating updates through a small public API. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect object relationships with ownership and lifetime before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.
